source.text: בַּלַּ֣יְלָה הַה֔וּא נָדְדָ֖ה שְׁנַ֣ת הַמֶּ֑לֶךְ וַיֹּ֗אמֶר לְהָבִ֞יא אֶת־סֵ֤פֶר הַזִּכְרֹנוֹת֙ דִּבְרֵ֣י הַיָּמִ֔ים וַיִּהְי֥וּ נִקְרָאִ֖ים לִפְנֵ֥י הַמֶּֽלֶךְ׃

records.literal_gloss: In the night the that fled [the] sleep of the king, and he said to bring the book of the records, [the] matters of the days, and they were being read before the king.

en.L: In that night the sleep of the king fled, and he said to bring the book of the records, the chronicles, and they were being read before the king.
en.B: That night the king could not sleep. So he ordered the book of records, the chronicles, to be brought, and they were read aloud to the king.
en.R: That night the king could not sleep. So he gave orders to bring the book that recorded the events of his reign, and it was read aloud to him.

decisions.choice: the king's sleep fled: the king could not sleep
decisions.reason: The Hebrew pictures sleep running away from the king. It means he lay awake (compare Genesis 31:40, where sleep "fled" from Jacob's eyes).

decisions.choice: the book of the records, the chronicles: the official record of the reign
decisions.reason: Literally "the book of the remembrances, the matters of the days". It is the royal chronicle in which Mordecai's report of the plot against the king was written down (2:23); the same kind of book is named again in 10:2. Keeping such records was part of Persian court life (Ezra 4:15; 6:1-2).

decisions.choice: that night: the night after Haman built the gallows for Mordecai
decisions.reason: The chapter opens on the same night that Haman, on his wife's advice, had the gallows made and planned to ask for Mordecai's death in the morning (5:14). The story sets the king's sleepless night beside Haman's plan without saying why it happened.

decisions.choice: they were being read: the reading went on for some time
decisions.reason: The verb with a participle describes ongoing action: the records were read, one after another, until the passage about Mordecai came up (verse 2).

decisions.choice: the king could not sleep
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable give the plain sense of the picture; Literal keeps "sleep fled".

decisions.choice: the book that recorded the events of his reign
decisions.reason: Readable explains what "the chronicles" were.

source.text: וַיִּמָּצֵ֣א כָת֗וּב אֲשֶׁר֩ הִגִּ֨יד מָרְדֳּכַ֜י עַל־בִּגְתָ֣נָא וָתֶ֗רֶשׁ שְׁנֵי֙ סָרִיסֵ֣י הַמֶּ֔לֶךְ מִשֹּׁמְרֵ֖י הַסַּ֑ף אֲשֶׁ֤ר בִּקְשׁוּ֙ לִשְׁלֹ֣חַ יָ֔ד בַּמֶּ֖לֶךְ אֲחַשְׁוֵרֽוֹשׁ׃

records.literal_gloss: And it was found written that had told Mordecai about Bigthana and Teresh, two of [the] eunuchs of the king, from [the] keepers of the threshold, who had sought to send a hand against the king Ahasuerus.

en.L: And it was found written that Mordecai had told about Bigthana and Teresh, two of the eunuchs of the king, from the keepers of the threshold, who had sought to lay a hand on King Ahasuerus.
en.B: There it was found written that Mordecai had exposed Bigthana and Teresh, two of the king's eunuchs who guarded the doorway, who had plotted to assassinate King Ahasuerus.
en.R: The record said that Mordecai had reported two of the king's palace officials, Bigthana and Teresh, who guarded the door. They had planned to kill King Ahasuerus.

decisions.choice: the plot told in 2:21-23
decisions.reason: This is the plot Mordecai uncovered while sitting at the king's gate. He told Esther, she told the king in Mordecai's name, the two men were hanged, and the matter was written in the chronicles (2:21-23). The first name is spelled Bigthan there and Bigthana here; both spellings are in the Hebrew text.

decisions.choice: keepers of the threshold: guards of the doors to the king's private rooms
decisions.reason: The title names officials who controlled the entrance to the king's quarters, which gave them close access to him and made the plot dangerous (2:21).

decisions.choice: sought to send a hand against: plotted to kill
decisions.reason: To "send a hand against" someone means to attack or kill him (1 Samuel 24:7; 26:9). Here it is a plot to assassinate the king.

decisions.choice: palace officials
decisions.reason: As throughout Esther, Readable says "palace officials" where Literal and Balanced say "eunuchs" (see 1:10).

source.text: וַיֹּ֣אמֶר הַמֶּ֔לֶךְ מַֽה־נַּעֲשָׂ֞ה יְקָ֧ר וּגְדוּלָּ֛ה לְמָרְדֳּכַ֖י עַל־זֶ֑ה וַיֹּ֨אמְר֜וּ נַעֲרֵ֤י הַמֶּ֨לֶךְ֙ מְשָׁ֣רְתָ֔יו לֹא־נַעֲשָׂ֥ה עִמּ֖וֹ דָּבָֽר׃

records.literal_gloss: And said the king, What has been done [of] honor and greatness for Mordecai for this? And said [the] young men of the king, his attendants, Not has been done with him anything.

en.L: And the king said, "What honor and greatness has been done for Mordecai for this?" And the young men of the king, his attendants, said, "Nothing has been done for him."
en.B: The king asked, "What honor or high rank has been given to Mordecai for this?" The young men who attended the king answered, "Nothing has been done for him."
en.R: The king asked, "What has been done to honor and reward Mordecai for this?" His servants answered, "Nothing at all has been done for him."

decisions.choice: honor and greatness: public honor and a rise in rank
decisions.reason: The two words are paired for a reward that brings both public esteem and higher standing. "Greatness" is used again of Mordecai's rank at the end of the book (10:2).

decisions.choice: a deed for the king was expected to be rewarded
decisions.reason: The king assumes that one who saved his life would have been rewarded. It is well attested that Persian kings recorded and rewarded those who did them service, and the question shows that in Mordecai's case this had been overlooked (2:23 says only that the matter was written down).

decisions.choice: the young men of the king, his attendants: the personal servants on duty with him
decisions.reason: The "young men" who "serve" the king are his personal attendants, the same group who give advice in 2:2. They are with him in the night.

decisions.choice: high rank
decisions.reason: "Greatness" in modern English sounds like a quality of character; Balanced says "high rank", the kind of greatness meant.

source.text: וַיֹּ֥אמֶר הַמֶּ֖לֶךְ מִ֣י בֶחָצֵ֑ר וְהָמָ֣ן בָּ֗א לַחֲצַ֤ר בֵּית־הַמֶּ֨לֶךְ֙ הַחִ֣יצוֹנָ֔ה לֵאמֹ֣ר לַמֶּ֔לֶךְ לִתְלוֹת֙ אֶֽת־מָרְדֳּכַ֔י עַל־הָעֵ֖ץ אֲשֶׁר־הֵכִ֥ין לֽוֹ׃

records.literal_gloss: And said the king, Who [is] in [the] court? And Haman had come to [the] court of [the] house of the king, the outer, to say to the king to hang Mordecai on the tree that he had prepared for him.

en.L: And the king said, "Who is in the court?" Now Haman had come into the outer court of the king's house to speak to the king about hanging Mordecai on the gallows that he had prepared for him.
en.B: The king said, "Who is in the court?" Now Haman had just entered the outer court of the palace to ask the king to have Mordecai hanged on the gallows he had set up for him.
en.R: The king asked, "Who is out in the courtyard?" Haman had just come into the outer courtyard of the palace. He had come to ask the king to hang Mordecai on the gallows that he had set up for him.

decisions.choice: hang on the tree: put to death and displayed on a tall wooden post
decisions.reason: The word translated "gallows" means "tree" or "wood"; in 5:14 it is a post fifty cubits high. "Hang" may mean hanging by the neck, impaling, or hanging up the body after death; the Persians are known to have impaled people (Ezra 6:11 threatens this). The text does not say which method is meant.

decisions.choice: Haman had come: he arrived at that moment
decisions.reason: The clause breaks into the story to say Haman had just arrived. He has come early, as his wife advised, to ask for Mordecai's death "in the morning" (5:14), at the very moment the king is thinking of how to reward Mordecai.

decisions.choice: the outer court: the courtyard outside the king's inner rooms
decisions.reason: No one could enter the inner court uninvited on pain of death (4:11). Haman waits in the outer court until the king calls him.

decisions.choice: the palace
decisions.reason: "The king's house" means the royal palace; Balanced and Readable say so.

source.text: וַיֹּ֨אמְר֜וּ נַעֲרֵ֤י הַמֶּ֨לֶךְ֙ אֵלָ֔יו הִנֵּ֥ה הָמָ֖ן עֹמֵ֣ד בֶּחָצֵ֑ר וַיֹּ֥אמֶר הַמֶּ֖לֶךְ יָבֽוֹא׃

records.literal_gloss: And said [the] young men of the king to him, Look, Haman standing in the court. And said the king, Let him come.

en.L: And the young men of the king said to him, "Look, Haman is standing in the court." And the king said, "Let him come in."
en.B: The king's attendants told him, "Haman is standing in the court." "Let him come in," the king said.
en.R: His servants answered, "Haman is standing out in the courtyard." The king said, "Tell him to come in."

decisions.choice: look: points to what is there
decisions.reason: The Hebrew word draws attention to what the speaker sees; here it simply presents Haman as the one waiting.

decisions.choice: "look" left unsaid
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable leave the pointing word unsaid, since natural English does not need it here; Literal keeps "look".

source.text: וַיָּבוֹא֮ הָמָן֒ וַיֹּ֤אמֶר לוֹ֙ הַמֶּ֔לֶךְ מַה־לַעֲשׂ֕וֹת בָּאִ֕ישׁ אֲשֶׁ֥ר הַמֶּ֖לֶךְ חָפֵ֣ץ בִּיקָר֑וֹ וַיֹּ֤אמֶר הָמָן֙ בְּלִבּ֔וֹ לְמִ֞י יַחְפֹּ֥ץ הַמֶּ֛לֶךְ לַעֲשׂ֥וֹת יְקָ֖ר יוֹתֵ֥ר מִמֶּֽנִּי׃

records.literal_gloss: And came Haman, and said to him the king, What to do for [the] man whom the king delights in his honor? And said Haman in his heart, To whom would delight the king to do honor more than me?

en.L: And Haman came in, and the king said to him, "What should be done for the man whom the king delights to honor?" And Haman said in his heart, "Whom would the king delight to honor more than me?"
en.B: When Haman came in, the king asked him, "What should be done for the man the king delights to honor?" Haman thought to himself, "Whom would the king delight to honor more than me?"
en.R: When Haman came in, the king asked him, "What should I do for a man I really want to honor?" Haman thought to himself, "Who is there that the king would want to honor more than me?"

decisions.choice: the man whom the king delights to honor: the king speaks of himself in the third person and names no one
decisions.reason: Speaking of "the king" instead of "I" is court style. The king does not say whom he means, and Haman, who does not know what was read in the night, assumes it is himself. The phrase is repeated four more times (verses 7, 9 twice, 11) and becomes the refrain of the scene.

decisions.choice: said in his heart: thought to himself
decisions.reason: In Hebrew one "says in the heart" what one thinks without saying it aloud (Genesis 17:17; Psalm 14:1).

decisions.choice: delight: to take pleasure in, to wish
decisions.reason: The verb means to take pleasure in something or someone and so to want it. It is the king's favor, not only a passing wish.

decisions.choice: What should I do for a man I really want to honor?
decisions.reason: Readable lets the king speak in the first person, since English readers may not see that "the king" means the speaker himself.

source.text: וַיֹּ֥אמֶר הָמָ֖ן אֶל־הַמֶּ֑לֶךְ אִ֕ישׁ אֲשֶׁ֥ר הַמֶּ֖לֶךְ חָפֵ֥ץ בִּיקָרֽוֹ׃

records.literal_gloss: And said Haman to the king, A man whom the king delights in his honor,

en.L: And Haman said to the king, "The man whom the king delights to honor,
en.B: Haman answered the king, "For the man the king delights to honor,
en.R: Haman answered the king, "Here is what to do for the man the king wants to honor.

decisions.choice: a broken-off beginning: the man is named first, then the proposal follows (verses 8-9)
decisions.reason: Haman begins by repeating the king's words and stops, then starts the sentence again with "let them bring" in verse 8. The broken sentence shows his eagerness. The sentence runs on into verses 8-9.

decisions.choice: Here is what to do for
decisions.reason: Readable smooths the broken sentence into a full one, so that verse 8 can begin a new sentence.

source.text: יָבִ֨יאוּ֙ לְב֣וּשׁ מַלְכ֔וּת אֲשֶׁ֥ר לָֽבַשׁ־בּ֖וֹ הַמֶּ֑לֶךְ וְס֗וּס אֲשֶׁ֨ר רָכַ֤ב עָלָיו֙ הַמֶּ֔לֶךְ וַאֲשֶׁ֥ר נִתַּ֛ן כֶּ֥תֶר מַלְכ֖וּת בְּרֹאשֽׁוֹ׃

records.literal_gloss: let them bring clothing of royalty that has worn it the king, and a horse that has ridden on it the king, and that has been put a crown of royalty on its head,

en.L: let them bring royal clothing that the king has worn, and a horse that the king has ridden, and on whose head a royal crown has been set,
en.B: let royal robes be brought that the king himself has worn, and a horse that the king has ridden, one with a royal crown placed on its head,
en.R: Have servants bring a royal robe that the king has worn and a horse that the king has ridden, with a royal crown on its head.

decisions.choice: the king's own robe and horse: sharing the king's honor in public
decisions.reason: To wear what the king has worn and ride what he has ridden is to be shown to everyone as the king's favorite. Joseph was honored in a similar way by Pharaoh (Genesis 41:42-43), and Solomon was set on David's own mule when he was made king (1 Kings 1:33). Haman asks for honor that comes close to the king's own.

decisions.choice: on its head: the crown is on the horse's head
alternatives: a royal crown placed on the head of the man the king honors
decisions.reason: The pronoun most naturally refers to the horse just mentioned: a royal horse with a crown-like crest on its head, as horses in Persian art sometimes have. It could instead mean that the crown is placed on the head of the honored man, but the crown is not mentioned again in verses 9-11, where the man is dressed and set on the horse.

decisions.choice: crown of royalty: a royal headdress
decisions.reason: This is the word used for the queen's crown (1:11; 2:17). On a horse it means an ornament or crest that marks it as the king's.

decisions.choice: Have servants bring
decisions.reason: Readable says who does the bringing, which the Hebrew leaves open ("let them bring").

source.text: וְנָת֨וֹן הַלְּב֜וּשׁ וְהַסּ֗וּס עַל־יַד־אִ֞ישׁ מִשָּׂרֵ֤י הַמֶּ֨לֶךְ֙ הַֽפַּרְתְּמִ֔ים וְהִלְבִּ֨ישׁוּ֙ אֶת־הָאִ֔ישׁ אֲשֶׁ֥ר הַמֶּ֖לֶךְ חָפֵ֣ץ בִּֽיקָר֑וֹ וְהִרְכִּיבֻ֤הוּ עַל־הַסּוּס֙ בִּרְח֣וֹב הָעִ֔יר וְקָרְא֣וּ לְפָנָ֔יו כָּ֚כָה יֵעָשֶׂ֣ה לָאִ֔ישׁ אֲשֶׁ֥ר הַמֶּ֖לֶךְ חָפֵ֥ץ בִּיקָרֽוֹ׃

records.literal_gloss: and let give the clothing and the horse into [the] hand of a man from [the] officials of the king, the nobles, and let them clothe the man whom the king delights in his honor, and let them make him ride on the horse in [the] square of the city, and let them call before him, Thus it is done for the man whom the king delights in his honor.

en.L: and let the clothing and the horse be given into the hand of one of the officials of the king, the nobles, and let them clothe the man whom the king delights to honor, and let them make him ride on the horse through the square of the city and call out before him, 'This is how it is done for the man whom the king delights to honor!'"
en.B: and let the robes and the horse be handed to one of the king's most noble officials. Let them dress the man the king delights to honor, lead him on horseback through the city square, and proclaim before him, 'This is what is done for the man the king delights to honor!'"
en.R: Then hand the robe and the horse over to one of the king's most important officials. Have him put the robe on the man the king wants to honor and lead him on the horse through the city square. Have him shout out ahead of him, 'This is what the king does for the man he wants to honor!'"

decisions.choice: the officials of the king, the nobles: one of the highest nobles
decisions.reason: The second word is a Persian word for the nobility, used for the great men at the king's first feast (1:3). Haman asks that the honored man be served by one of the highest men in the kingdom, never thinking it will be himself.

decisions.choice: a public parade and proclamation in the city square
decisions.reason: The open square near the gate was the city's public place (Nehemiah 8:1). Leading a man through it while a herald calls out made his honor known to everyone, as when Joseph rode in Pharaoh's chariot and people called out before him (Genesis 41:43).

decisions.choice: make him ride: set him on the horse and lead him
decisions.reason: The verb means to cause someone to ride. The noble walks and leads the horse, while the honored man rides.

decisions.choice: lead him on horseback; lead him on the horse
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable say what "make him ride" means in this scene; Literal keeps the causative verb.

decisions.choice: This is what the king does for the man he wants to honor
decisions.reason: Readable names the king as the one who honors, which the passive "it is done" implies.

source.text: וַיֹּ֨אמֶר הַמֶּ֜לֶךְ לְהָמָ֗ן מַ֠הֵר קַ֣ח אֶת־הַלְּב֤וּשׁ וְאֶת־הַסּוּס֙ כַּאֲשֶׁ֣ר דִּבַּ֔רְתָּ וַֽעֲשֵׂה־כֵן֙ לְמָרְדֳּכַ֣י הַיְּהוּדִ֔י הַיּוֹשֵׁ֖ב בְּשַׁ֣עַר הַמֶּ֑לֶךְ אַל־תַּפֵּ֣ל דָּבָ֔ר מִכֹּ֖ל אֲשֶׁ֥ר דִּבַּֽרְתָּ׃

records.literal_gloss: And said the king to Haman, Hurry, take the clothing and the horse as you have spoken, and do so to Mordecai the Jew, the [one] sitting in [the] gate of the king; not let fall a word from all that you have spoken.

en.L: And the king said to Haman, "Hurry, take the clothing and the horse, as you have said, and do so for Mordecai the Jew, who sits in the king's gate. Do not let a word fall from all that you have said."
en.B: Then the king said to Haman, "Hurry! Take the robes and the horse just as you have said, and do this for Mordecai the Jew, who sits at the king's gate. Do not leave out anything you have proposed."
en.R: Then the king told Haman, "Hurry! Get the robe and the horse, just as you said, and do all this for Mordecai the Jew, who serves at the king's gate. Do not leave out a single thing you have suggested."

decisions.choice: sitting in the king's gate: holding a post at the royal gate
decisions.reason: The gate of the palace was where officials of the court did their work. Mordecai has sat there since 2:19-21, and there he refused to bow to Haman (3:2; 5:9, 13).

decisions.choice: not let a word fall: leave nothing undone
decisions.reason: A "word" that "falls" is one that is not carried out (Joshua 21:45; 1 Samuel 3:19). The king tells Haman to do every part of what he proposed.

decisions.choice: Mordecai the Jew: the king knows who Mordecai is
decisions.reason: The king names Mordecai and his people. Haman must now honor the man he came to have put to death, and a Jew, whose people Haman has arranged to destroy (3:6, 13). The text does not say whether the king connects this with the decree he allowed.

decisions.choice: serves at the king's gate
decisions.reason: Readable says "serves" so the reader does not picture Mordecai as idle; "sitting" in the gate means holding office there.

source.text: וַיִּקַּ֤ח הָמָן֙ אֶת־הַלְּב֣וּשׁ וְאֶת־הַסּ֔וּס וַיַּלְבֵּ֖שׁ אֶֽת־מָרְדֳּכָ֑י וַיַּרְכִּיבֵ֨הוּ֙ בִּרְח֣וֹב הָעִ֔יר וַיִּקְרָ֣א לְפָנָ֔יו כָּ֚כָה יֵעָשֶׂ֣ה לָאִ֔ישׁ אֲשֶׁ֥ר הַמֶּ֖לֶךְ חָפֵ֥ץ בִּיקָרֽוֹ׃

records.literal_gloss: And took Haman the clothing and the horse, and he clothed Mordecai, and he made him ride in [the] square of the city, and he called before him, Thus it is done for the man whom the king delights in his honor.

en.L: And Haman took the clothing and the horse, and he clothed Mordecai and made him ride through the square of the city, and he called out before him, "This is how it is done for the man whom the king delights to honor!"
en.B: So Haman took the robes and the horse. He dressed Mordecai, led him on horseback through the city square, and proclaimed before him, "This is what is done for the man the king delights to honor!"
en.R: So Haman got the robe and the horse. He put the robe on Mordecai and led him on the horse through the city square. He shouted out ahead of him, "This is what the king does for the man he wants to honor!"

decisions.choice: Haman himself does it all
decisions.reason: Every verb has Haman as its subject. He proposed that one of the nobles serve the honored man (verse 9), and now he is that noble, calling out his own words about Mordecai.

decisions.choice: led him on horseback; led him on the horse
decisions.reason: As in verse 9, Balanced and Readable say what "made him ride" means.

source.text: וַיָּ֥שָׁב מָרְדֳּכַ֖י אֶל־שַׁ֣עַר הַמֶּ֑לֶךְ וְהָמָן֙ נִדְחַ֣ף אֶל־בֵּית֔וֹ אָבֵ֖ל וַחֲפ֥וּי רֹֽאשׁ׃

records.literal_gloss: And returned Mordecai to [the] gate of the king, and Haman hurried to his house, mourning and covered of head.

en.L: And Mordecai returned to the king's gate, but Haman hurried to his house, mourning and with his head covered.
en.B: Then Mordecai returned to the king's gate, but Haman hurried home, grieving, with his head covered.
en.R: Afterward Mordecai went back to the king's gate. But Haman rushed home with his head covered, full of grief and shame.

decisions.choice: mourning and with covered head: a sign of grief and shame
decisions.reason: Covering the head was a sign of grief or humiliation (2 Samuel 15:30; Jeremiah 14:3-4). Haman goes home as a mourner on the day he expected to triumph.

decisions.choice: Mordecai returns, Haman hurries: two men going opposite ways
decisions.reason: The verse sets the two side by side. Mordecai goes quietly back to his post at the gate, unchanged by the honor; Haman rushes home. The verb used for Haman means to hurry or be driven on.

decisions.choice: full of grief and shame
decisions.reason: Readable says what the covered head showed, since modern readers may not know the custom.

source.text: וַיְסַפֵּ֨ר הָמָ֜ן לְזֶ֤רֶשׁ אִשְׁתּוֹ֙ וּלְכָל־אֹ֣הֲבָ֔יו אֵ֖ת כָּל־אֲשֶׁ֣ר קָרָ֑הוּ וַיֹּ֩אמְרוּ֩ל֨וֹ חֲכָמָ֜יו וְזֶ֣רֶשׁ אִשְׁתּ֗וֹ אִ֣ם מִזֶּ֣רַע הַיְּהוּדִ֡ים מָרְדֳּכַ֞י אֲשֶׁר֩ הַחִלּ֨וֹתָ לִנְפֹּ֤ל לְפָנָיו֙ לֹא־תוּכַ֣ל ל֔וֹ כִּֽי־נָפ֥וֹל תִּפּ֖וֹל לְפָנָֽיו׃

records.literal_gloss: And recounted Haman to Zeresh his wife and to all his friends all that had happened to him. And said to him his wise [men] and Zeresh his wife, If from [the] seed of the Jews [is] Mordecai, before whom you have begun to fall, not you will prevail against him, but falling you will fall before him.

en.L: And Haman recounted to Zeresh his wife and to all his friends all that had happened to him. And his wise men and Zeresh his wife said to him, "If Mordecai, before whom you have begun to fall, is from the seed of the Jews, you will not prevail against him, but you will surely fall before him."
en.B: Haman told his wife Zeresh and all his friends everything that had happened to him. His advisers and his wife Zeresh said to him, "If Mordecai, before whom you have begun to fall, is of Jewish descent, you will not get the better of him. You will certainly fall before him."
en.R: Haman told his wife Zeresh and all his friends everything that had happened to him. His advisers and his wife Zeresh said to him, "You have already started to lose to Mordecai. If he is a Jew, you cannot win against him. You will certainly be ruined by him."

decisions.choice: his friends, then his wise men: the same circle of advisers
decisions.reason: The people Haman calls his friends (as in 5:10, 14) are now called his "wise men", that is, his counselors. The word recalls the king's wise men who advised him in 1:13.

decisions.choice: if Mordecai is of Jewish descent: a condition they treat as known
alternatives: since Mordecai is of Jewish descent
decisions.reason: Haman already knows Mordecai is a Jew (3:4-6), so the "if" does not express doubt; it states the ground of what follows: since he is of that people, Haman cannot win.

decisions.choice: why the Jews cannot be overcome: the speakers give no reason
decisions.reason: Haman's advisers do not say why a man of the Jews cannot be defeated. Some readers hear an echo of the old enmity between Israel and Amalek, which ends in Amalek's defeat (Exodus 17:14-16; 1 Samuel 15), since Haman is called the Agagite (3:1); others see a hint that Israel's God protects his people. The book does not name God, and the text leaves the reason unstated.

decisions.choice: fall ... surely fall: the verb repeated for emphasis
decisions.reason: The verb "fall" is used three times: Haman has begun to fall, and he will surely fall, using a doubled verb that stresses certainty. The fall begun today will be complete.

decisions.choice: his advisers
decisions.reason: "Wise men" here means counselors; Balanced and Readable say "advisers" so it does not sound like praise of their wisdom.

decisions.choice: be ruined by him
decisions.reason: Readable gives the sense of "fall before him", total defeat.

source.text: עוֹדָם֙ מְדַבְּרִ֣ים עִמּ֔וֹ וְסָרִיסֵ֥י הַמֶּ֖לֶךְ הִגִּ֑יעוּ וַיַּבְהִ֨לוּ֙ לְהָבִ֣יא אֶת־הָמָ֔ן אֶל־הַמִּשְׁתֶּ֖ה אֲשֶׁר־עָשְׂתָ֥ה אֶסְתֵּֽר׃

records.literal_gloss: Still they [were] speaking with him, and [the] eunuchs of the king arrived and hurried to bring Haman to the feast that had made Esther.

en.L: While they were still speaking with him, the eunuchs of the king arrived, and they hurried to bring Haman to the feast that Esther had prepared.
en.B: While they were still talking with him, the king's eunuchs arrived and hurried Haman off to the banquet Esther had prepared.
en.R: While they were still talking, the king's palace officials arrived. They rushed Haman off to the banquet that Esther had prepared.

decisions.choice: the eunuchs come to escort Haman to the banquet
decisions.reason: Haman had already been invited to Esther's second banquet (5:8, 12). Guests of the court were escorted by royal servants. Their haste leaves him no time to recover.

decisions.choice: feast: a banquet of wine
decisions.reason: The word comes from the verb "to drink" and names a banquet where wine was served (5:6; 7:2, 7).

decisions.choice: palace officials
decisions.reason: Readable says "palace officials" for the eunuchs, as elsewhere in Esther (see 1:10).
